questions.q: Define Biological Value (BV) and Net Protein Utilization (NPU) and state the relationship between them.
questions.a: BV = (Nitrogen retained / Nitrogen absorbed) × 100; NPU = (Nitrogen retained / Nitrogen intake) × 100. Since absorbed nitrogen ≤ intake nitrogen, BV ≥ NPU always. A wrong answer that swaps the denominators or claims NPU > BV reveals confusion between absorption and intake steps in nitrogen metabolism.

questions.q: A student says: "Plant proteins are always incomplete and animal proteins are always complete." Explain why this statement is incorrect using two specific counterexamples.
questions.a: Soy protein (plant) is complete (contains all essential amino acids in adequate proportions), while gelatin (animal) is incomplete (lacks tryptophan). The error arises from overgeneralising source-based classification; completeness depends on amino acid profile, not source alone. A wrong answer that repeats the statement shows lack of nuance in nutritional quality assessment.

questions.q: Calculate BV and NPU for a subject who consumed 20g protein (16% nitrogen), absorbed 15g protein equivalent, and retained 12g protein equivalent. Show all steps.
questions.a:
Step 1: Convert protein to nitrogen: Intake N = 20g × 0.16 = 3.2g N. Absorbed N = 15g × 0.16 = 2.4g N. Retained N = 12g × 0.16 = 1.92g N.
Step 2: BV = (1.92 / 2.4) × 100 = 80%. NPU = (1.92 / 3.2) × 100 = 60%.
Step 3: Verify BV > NPU (80% > 60%). A wrong answer that forgets the 16% conversion factor or uses protein grams directly in the formula reveals misunderstanding of nitrogen as the measured unit.

questions.q: Compare the protein quality of a diet providing 60% protein from cereals and 40% from pulses versus a diet providing 100% protein from milk, using the concept of mutual supplementation and BV.
questions.a: Cereals are lysine-deficient but methionine-rich; pulses are methionine-deficient but lysine-rich. Together they complement each other, raising the combined BV closer to milk (BV ~90%). Milk alone has high BV (~90%) due to complete amino acid profile. The cereal-pulse blend (typical Indian diet) can achieve BV ~70-75% after supplementation. A wrong answer that claims cereal-pulse blend equals milk BV ignores limiting amino acid kinetics and digestibility differences.

questions.q: Critique the use of BV alone for evaluating protein quality in a weight-loss diet where energy intake is restricted.
questions.a: BV measures nitrogen retention when protein is the sole nitrogen source and energy is adequate. Under energy restriction, protein is diverted for gluconeogenesis, lowering nitrogen retention artificially; thus BV underestimates true protein quality. NPU or PER under controlled energy conditions is more appropriate. A wrong answer that says BV is always reliable ignores the energy-protein interaction, a classic competitive exam trap.

questions.q: Design a one-day vegetarian menu for a 60 kg adolescent (protein requirement 1g/kg) that achieves at least 70% BV through mutual supplementation. List foods, protein grams, and explain the supplementation logic.
questions.a: Menu: Breakfast – 2 idli (4g) + sambar (3g) = 7g (rice + urad dal); Lunch – 2 chapati (6g) + 1 katori rajma (7g) = 13g (wheat + kidney bean); Snack – 1 glass soy milk (7g); Dinner – 1 katori khichdi (rice+moong dal, 8g) + curd (4g) = 12g. Total = 39g protein (target 60g, but demonstrates principle). Supplementation: cereal (lysine-low) + pulse (methionine-low) at each meal; soy milk and curd add complete proteins. A poor answer that lists only cereals or only pulses shows failure to apply mutual supplementation concept.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Proteins are ______ composed of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, classified based on structure (simple, conjugated, derived), source (animal, plant), and nutritional quality (complete, incomplete); their quality is assessed using indices such as Biological Value (BV) and Net Protein Utilization (NPU) which measure nitrogen retention relative to absorption and intake respectively.
Fill in the blank: Start by asking: "Why do two people eating the same grams of protein from dal and egg have different muscle-building ______?" This hooks the student to protein quality.
What is Proteins? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Proteins are macromolecules composed of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, classified based on structure (simple, conjugated, derived), source (animal, plant), and nutritional quality (complete, incomplete); their quality is assessed using indices such as Biological Value (BV) and Net Protein Utilization (NPU) which measure nitrogen.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Proteins?
questions.a: Students often think "Biological Value measures how much protein is absorbed" – confusing absorption with retention.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) classify proteins by structure, source, and nutritional quality with examples, (2) explain at least five physiological functions of proteins, and (3) calculate BV and NPU from given nitrogen balance data, interpreting the results for dietary planning.
